claimText: The default match-score threshold for OpenSanctions-backed screening (above which a candidate is surfaced as a match) is 0.7, and the default algorithm is calibrated to be used with that value.

claimText: A match query is processed in two stages: first a search index locates candidate results optimized for recall (retrieval), then those candidates are evaluated against the query using the configured matching algorithm (scoring).

claimText: OpenSanctions' regression-v1 matching algorithm scores candidates across exactly 18 named features (e.g. name_match, name_token_overlap, name_levenshtein, dob_matches, dob_year_matches, dob_year_disjoint, identifier_match, org_identifier_match, address_match, gender_mismatch, country_mismatch, and others), confirmed by manual count of the published feature table, not name similarity alone.

claimText: The name-based and name-qualified algorithms compare names using Jaro-Winkler string similarity combined with Soundex phonetic matching, are both deprecated in favour of the ofac (OFACMatcher) algorithm, and OpenSanctions' own documentation states neither reaches parity with OFAC's public Sanctions List Search tool.

source.title: OpenSanctions Matcher: Deprecated Matching Algorithms

claimText: A separate algorithm (ofac / OFACMatcher) is reverse-engineered from OFAC's own scoring FAQ (FAQ #249) and parity fixtures captured against the live public tool, specifically to emulate sanctionssearch.ofac.treas.gov's behaviour, distinct from the deprecated name-based and name-qualified algorithms.

source.title: OpenSanctions Matcher: ofac Algorithm

claimText: logic-v2 is a deterministic, rule-based matching algorithm whose name matcher uses curated, multilingual cultural reference data for cross-language and cross-script matching, and OpenSanctions' own API tuning documentation recommends pinning to logic-v2 for new integrations.

claimText: MLR 2017 Part 7A does not gate on a monetary threshold. (1) Perimeter: Part 7A applies only to a 'cryptoasset transfer' as defined in Reg 64B, either a transfer between cryptoasset businesses or an unhosted wallet transfer as there defined. (2) Exclusions, not threshold-based: Reg 64A(2) excludes transfers within Article 3.9 of the funds transfer regulation; Reg 64A(3) excludes transfers where both originator and beneficiary are cryptoasset businesses acting on their own behalf. (3) Universal base requirement: Reg 64C(1) and (5) require the originator's business to attach both parties' names, registered/trading name for any party that is a firm, and account numbers or a unique transaction identifier for both originator and beneficiary, with no monetary threshold; the transfer must not proceed without it (Reg 64C(9)); a narrow batch-file exception under Reg 64C(7) lets qualifying transfers to a beneficiary business wholly outside the UK carry this information at the batch level. (4) Additional (paragraph 6) information runs on two separate routes: Reg 64C(2), no threshold, applies where every executing business operates in the UK and the beneficiary's business requests it (3 working day response); Reg 64C(4) applies where not every executing business is UK-based, and requires the extra information once the transfer, aggregated with linked transfers, meets or exceeds £800 (amended from EUR 1,000 by SI 2026/621 reg 32, effective 30 June 2026); for an individual originator, paragraph (6) is alternatives (customer ID number, address, identity document number, or date/place of birth), not a cumulative list. (5) Unhosted wallet transfers run under a separate rule, Reg 64G, with their own £800 threshold (amended from EUR 1,000 by the same SI 2026/621, reg 33) for enhanced information, distinct from the Reg 64C(4) threshold.

source.title: MLR 2017 Part 7A (regs 64A-64H); Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/621), regs 32 and 33 (threshold amendments, effective 30 June 2026)

claimText: US jurisdiction only, no UK obligation. FinCEN issued a Section 311 (USA PATRIOT Act) final rule against Huione Group, a Cambodia-based (Phnom Penh) financial conglomerate with subsidiaries Huione Pay PLC, Huione Crypto and Haowang Guarantee (formerly Huione Guarantee), issued 14 October 2025, effective 17 November 2025, after finding reasonable grounds that Huione Group was a foreign financial institution of primary money laundering concern. The rule's scope is three-part: a prohibition on covered US financial institutions opening or maintaining a US correspondent account for Huione Group; a requirement to take reasonable steps preventing indirect processing of Huione Group transactions through covered correspondent accounts; and a requirement for specified special due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts. FinCEN's stated grounds are kept separate, not blended: (1) Huione Group services used by DPRK government entities to launder proceeds of cyber heists; (2) use by Southeast Asian criminal organisations to launder proceeds of cyber scams, including convertible virtual currency investment scams such as 'pig butchering'; and (3) Huione Group's operation of an illicit online market. FinCEN's own primary text states directly: 'FinCEN's analysis identified that, in the aggregate, Huione Group has received at least USD 4 billion worth of illicit proceeds, between August 2021 and January 2025.' This figure is confirmed against FinCEN's primary text, superseding this guide's earlier note that it was unconfirmed. Huione Pay PLC was previously a registered Cambodian payment services institution; by 2025 its licence had been rescinded by the National Bank of Cambodia and it no longer appeared in the Ministry of Commerce's business registration database. In June 2026, FinCEN proposed adding H Pay Service PLC and successor entities to the definition; as at August 2026 this remains a proposed amendment, not part of the operative 2025 final rule. Independently verified this session via WebSearch and WebFetch against FinCEN.gov and the Federal Register's full text, and corroborated by Money Laundering Watch (Ballard Spahr); this case study was not present in the original draft, which referenced it without a source or citable content, so it was sourced from scratch rather than carried over. claimText: FinCrimeRadar interpretive analysis, not a direct quotation of statute: "cryptoasset exchange provider" and "custodian wallet provider" are pre-existing MLR 2017 registration categories defined by regulation 14A. SI 2026/621 cross-references regulation 14A throughout as an already-existing provision (it inserts regulation 34A and substitutes Schedule 6B, but never inserts or amends 14A itself), which independently confirms 14A pre-dates this instrument; the specific attribution of regulation 14A's insertion to SI 2019/1511 rests on a compiler's annotation in the retrieved extract, not on independently checked SI 2019/1511 text, and should be reconfirmed directly at drafting time. MLR registration under regulation 14A runs under a different regulatory basis (registration) than the new FSMA-authorised activities created by SI 2026/102 (RAO Chapter 2B, articles 9M-9Z6, authorisation under FSMA Part 4A). These are two parallel regimes with different populations and different legal bases, not one continuous regime with a single transition date: SI 2026/621 alone carries three separate commencement dates for cryptoasset-relevant provisions (regulation 34A: 1 February 2027; Schedule 6B paragraphs 1/2/5: approximately 30 June 2026; Schedule 6B paragraphs 3/4: 25 October 2027; general MLR housekeeping: approximately 30 June 2026), none of which is a single unified transition date, and none of which is the same as SI 2026/102's own commencement structure (21-day preparatory commencement, full commencement 25 October 2027) except by coincidental overlap on 25 October 2027 for the Schedule 6B post-registration cohort. SI 2026/621 layers additional obligations onto the existing MLR registration regime rather than creating cryptoasset AML regulation from scratch, confirmed structurally by the instrument's own drafting: regulation 34A is inserted as genuinely new text, but Schedule 6B is expressly "substituted" for an existing Schedule 6B, which is direct textual proof that a cryptoasset-relevant Schedule 6B, and by extension a cryptoasset AML framework, already existed before SI 2026/621.

claimText: Regulation 34A, inserted into MLR 2017 by SI 2026/621 regulation 20, applies to a cryptoasset exchange provider or custodian wallet provider ("correspondent") with a correspondent relationship, involving services of the type described in regulation 14A(1) or (2), with another similar-services provider from a third country ("respondent"). In addition to existing regulation 33 measures, it requires: gathering sufficient information to understand the respondent's business fully; determining the respondent's reputation and supervision quality from publicly-available credible sources; assessing the respondent's AML/CTF controls; senior management approval before establishing a new correspondent relationship; documenting the responsibilities of respondent and correspondent; and being satisfied that, for the respondent's direct-access customers, the respondent has verified identity and conducts ongoing CDD, and can produce that CDD documentation on request. Regulation 34A(2) separately prohibits cryptoasset exchange providers and custodian wallet providers from entering into or continuing a correspondent relationship with a shell bank outright. Regulation 34A(3) requires appropriate enhanced measures to avoid correspondent relationships with a credit or financial institution known to allow its accounts to be used by a shell bank. claimText: CASS 8 (mandate rules) does not apply to a firm safeguarding cryptoassets within the meaning of Article 9N. The FCA draws this distinction on its own terms: CASS 8's concept of "control" relates to a firm's authority to instruct or direct a client's assets, whereas Article 9N's concept of "control" relates to a firm's ability to bring about a transfer of benefit of a client's cryptoassets; these are different tests despite shared vocabulary. A CASS 8 mandate over cryptoassets (e.g. a discretionary investment manager's power of attorney) can still exist, but the mandate-holder in that scenario is not the Article 9N safeguarding firm, it is in a position to instruct the safeguarding firm instead. Whether CASS 8 applies to non-custodial staking (staking without safeguarding) depends on whether the firm holds mandate authority to instruct in relation to the relevant assets, meeting all conditions in CASS 8.2.1R(1)-(5); the FCA states most existing non-custodial staking models do not currently involve this type of authority.

claimText: The saving provision under SI 2026/102 protects a firm that applied for authorisation (or variation of permission) within the 30 September 2026 to 28 February 2027 application window whose application is not yet finally determined at full commencement (25 October 2027), including where the firm has referred an FCA refusal to the Upper Tribunal and the Tribunal has not yet made a final decision. Such a firm may continue providing cryptoasset services, not merely wind them down, until the application is finally determined. The firm must notify the FCA that it is using the saving provision as soon as reasonably practicable after full commencement, and must notify the FCA again when it ceases using it. Even during an open Upper Tribunal referral, the FCA may direct the firm into the transitional provision instead of the saving provision where it considers this necessary for preventing, detecting, investigating or prosecuting a criminal offence, for consumer protection, or for advancing the FCA's objectives; and if the Tribunal ultimately upholds the FCA's refusal, the firm then moves into the transitional provision to exit the market in an orderly manner. This is a distinct, separate mechanism from the transitional provision; the two must not be collapsed into one "savings provisions" concept.

claimText: The transitional provision under SI 2026/102 is a distinct, more restrictive mechanism than the saving provision, permitting wind-down/run-off only: it exempts an eligible firm from the s.19 FSMA general prohibition, or from s.20 FSMA for firms already FSMA-authorised, but only in respect of the new cryptoasset regulated activities and only to the extent necessary to perform a pre-existing contract entered into before the firm entered the provision. Firms in the provision cannot enter new contracts with existing or new UK customers. Eligibility is a two-factor test combining application-window timing with whether the application is still live at commencement, not window timing alone: an out-of-window applicant (applied after the window closed but before full commencement) whose application is undetermined at commencement enters the transitional provision automatically by operation of law; an in-window applicant whose application is finally refused with no live Tribunal review, or who withdraws, before commencement also falls into the transitional provision, not the saving provision, because nothing live remains at commencement for the saving provision to protect. Firms that never apply get neither mechanism and must run off before commencement or risk an s.19/s.20 FSMA breach. Maximum wind-down period is two years from full commencement (25 October 2027); continuing regulated activity after that risks an s.19/s.20 FSMA breach. Requires notification to the FCA on entering the provision and again on ceasing use, including on completing run-off, and requires notification to each counterparty of a pre-existing contract disclosing use of the provision, unauthorised status, and any material change to asset protection, dispute resolution, or compensation scheme availability for that contract. Financial promotions while in the provision are restricted to what is necessary to perform pre-existing contracts. The FCA retains power to amend the scope of a firm's exemption (e.g. removing a regulated activity from it), impose conditions, cancel the exemption, gather information, publish information about firms using the provision, and publicly censure a firm that fails to notify or acts contrary to the FCA's objectives. Background, not independently verified against MLR 2017's own registration text in this pass: MLR-registered firms do not automatically convert to FSMA authorisation and must apply fresh; firms already FSMA-authorised for other activities need a variation of permission rather than a new application.

claimText: Reserve composition: core backing assets are short-term deposits and short-term government debt instruments. The on-demand deposit requirement (ODDR) is 5% of the backing pool, on-demand deposits only, and applies to all UK stablecoin issuers. Expanded backing assets (longer-dated government debt, PDCNAV MMFs, repurchase agreements) are permitted with FCA notification and compliance with the Backing Asset Composition Requirement (BACR, renamed from "Ratio"). BACR and CBAR are distinct terms, not interchangeable: firms must calculate a Core Backing Asset Requirement (CBAR) equal to the higher of 5% of the backing pool or the highest daily redemption percentage in the past 180 redemption days (or since CASS 16 applied to the product if fewer), calculated on every redemption day (increased from the originally proposed 14-day interval); ODDR-satisfying deposits cannot double-count toward CBAR. Single-currency backing only: a UK-issued qualifying stablecoin may only be backed by assets in its denominated currency; multi-currency stablecoins are entirely out of scope of "qualifying stablecoin" (cross-referencing Article 88G, already independently verified in commit c2871a8, not re-verified here). Up to 5% excess is permitted in the backing pool following internal reconciliation, subject to the statutory trust. Full 1:1 backing is required at all times, including issuer-held stablecoins; the only exception is stablecoins permanently burned or removed from the pool. Reserve custodian, corrected from the original consultation proposal: the FCA originally proposed requiring third-party custodians unconnected to the issuer's group, but the final rule changed this after 60% of consultation responses were unsupportive. Intragroup custodians are now permitted, subject to a 20% cap on backing pool value (modelled on the CASS 7 approach to client money deposit diversification); firms may exceed the cap only where they demonstrate, after assessment, that compliance would be disproportionate given the pool's low value and business nature/scale/complexity relative to the safety offered by third-party custodians, and must notify the FCA before relying on this exemption and keep the assessment under periodic review. Firms must comply with SYSC 10 conflicts-of-interest obligations, periodically review custodian-diversification need across all custodians including intragroup ones, and maintain a prudent custody policy avoiding excessive concentration with any single custodian or group. Signed acknowledgement letters are required from each custodian before backing assets are held with them, a single letter per custodian covering all relevant accounts is sufficient, electronic letters are permitted per CASS 16 Annex 2.12G using the mandatory wording in CASS 16 Annex 1R, and letters must be reviewed at least annually and on any relevant change. Guide 1 must not present "independent custodian" as an absolute requirement.

claimText: Redemption rights and redemption eligibility, corrected from the original consultation proposal: there is a universal right to redeem UK-issued qualifying stablecoins at par value, but the T+1 redemption timeline's trigger point changed between consultation and final rule. It now commences when the issuer receives the stablecoin being redeemed in its own wallet, not from the redemption request as originally proposed, meaning AML/KYC obligations must be completed before the T+1 clock starts, not within the T+1 window. The T+1 timeline does not apply where compliance would breach money laundering legislation; issuers may rely on MLR regulation 39 (reliance on authorised third parties) for KYC checks performed by a limited set of other firms. A contract must be in place between the issuer and each person to whom it issues stablecoins, incorporating the redemption conditions, and the redemption obligation must pass effectively in law from one holder to the next to support secondary-market holders' redemption rights as well as original purchasers'; issuers are not mandated to use a specific legal mechanism, deed polls, novation, assignment, open offer, and clear website terms are all cited as acceptable options. Reserve disclosure: information likely to change frequently (stablecoins in circulation, backing pool value) must be updated at least every three months as a minimum baseline; more static information (risks, redemption fees) must be updated whenever it becomes inaccurate or misleading. Firms disclose backing assets only by asset-type category, no individual-position breakdown required, and there is no prescribed format or template for website disclosures. A five-year retention requirement applies, with earlier disclosure versions provided to tokenholders and relevant former holders on request. Only custodians holding more than 20% of the backing pool must be named in disclosures, not all custodians. A Digital Token Identifier (DTI) under ISO 24165, or an equivalent alternative identifier, must be disclosed. A Stablecoin QCDD is required before sale or subscription to prospective holders, content aligned to at least match website disclosures, updated at the same frequency as far as reasonably practicable. PS26/10 itself states that, under Regulation 12 of SI 2026/102, the issuer remains solely responsible for QCDD content, accuracy and updates, not transferring to a UK QCATP or other third party admitting the stablecoin to trading; Regulation 12's own primary legislative text has not itself been independently retrieved or checked this session (only Regulation 13 was, in an earlier commit), so this specific point rests on PS26/10's own authoritative restatement of Regulation 12, not on independently checked SI 2026/102 primary text, and should be cross-checked directly against Regulation 12 if it becomes load-bearing for drafting.

claimText: Independent assurance IS FCA-mandated, correcting commit 57c3045's Category 2 classification, which wrongly grouped it with fields having no FCA disclosure basis. Per PS26/10 paras 9.10-9.14, UK stablecoin issuers must obtain an annual independent review of the accuracy of statements made in the previous 12 months regarding the 1:1 ratio between the backing asset pool and the stablecoin pool. The review must be prepared in line with a "reasonable assurance engagement" standard, by a person meeting FCA-specified qualifications not limited to Companies Act auditors; crypto-specific technical, custody, valuation or systems-assurance expertise is explicitly accepted, including non-UK qualifications. As soon as practicable following the review, firms must publish a statement prepared by the reviewer stating the outcome, review date, and qualifications. A specific SMF (e.g. Compliance Officer SMF16, or the CASS oversight officer) must be designated responsible for the quarterly disclosure declaration. The FCA explicitly rejected alternative approaches raised in consultation (on-chain verification, reliance on existing financial statements, more frequent oversight) as providing a lower level of assurance than an independent review.

claimText: Closes the sourcing gap flagged in commit ae75c13 and left open through 3a14c6e (stablecoin-series-guide-1.issuer-entity-jurisdiction-partial.001). The FCA's default expectation under the AICF (Approach to International Cryptoasset Firms) non-Handbook guidance is that international cryptoasset firms will operate through a UK legal entity, not a branch; this expectation applies specifically to firms that are solo-regulated by the FCA. Dual-regulated firms (FCA and PRA) are the exception: they may operate cryptoasset activities from a UK branch instead if they demonstrate at the authorisation gateway, and on an ongoing basis, that they meet the threshold conditions from that branch, assessed case-by-case, with the PRA as lead regulator for those firms. Guide 1's "regulatory status" due diligence field should prompt practitioners to check which regulatory category, solo- or dual-regulated, a given issuer falls into before assuming the UK-legal-entity default applies. This guidance applies to three distinct starting positions: firms already FSMA-authorised for other activities needing a variation of permission, crypto MLR-registered firms not yet FSMA-authorised, and firms currently using the "section 21 gateway" not yet FSMA-authorised or MLR-registered. The FCA's own finalised guidance sits in FG26/7, referenced but not itself retrieved this session; treat FG26/7 as the next-level source if anything more granular becomes needed.
